script.opening: "Thank you for seeing me. I know I’ve been in a lot, but this time I’m really worried — the headaches, my heart races, I get tingling, I’m exhausted. I’ve read it could be a brain tumour or MS. I know my last scan was normal but that was weeks ago, things change, don’t they? I really think I need another scan, or to see a neurologist, just to be completely sure. I can’t relax until I know it’s not something serious."

facts.text: If explored: months of generalised, free-floating worry (not just about health), muscle tension, restlessness, poor sleep, irritability, fatigue, and somatic anxiety symptoms (palpitations, tingling/paraesthesia from hyperventilation, tension headaches). Repeated normal investigations; reassurance helps only briefly before the worry re-attaches to a new symptom/diagnosis. This is health anxiety, often with underlying generalised anxiety disorder (the GAD features above as described in NICE CG113, 2011).

She seeks scans/specialists for certainty; each normal result calms her only fleetingly, then doubt returns ("things change"). Repeated testing and reassurance REINFORCE the anxiety cycle. The challenge is to redirect from "more tests" to treating the anxiety — without dismissing her or missing genuine new pathology.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the health anxiety crystallised after a close FRIEND DIED SUDDENLY last year (a brain aneurysm/"young and healthy"), and Nadia is terrified the same will happen to her, leaving her own children motherless. The bodily checking and scan-seeking are attempts to control that terror. She hasn’t connected the bereavement to her symptoms. There may be guilt/grief she hasn’t processed.

If reached: the constant worry and checking are exhausting her, straining her marriage ("he says I’m obsessed"), and she feels ashamed and out of control — but more scans feel like the only relief. Validating the distress as real (the symptoms ARE real, anxiety causes them) is key.

Officially: another scan / a neurologist for certainty. What she needs: a confident, validating explanation linking her real symptoms to anxiety, the reassurance/testing cycle gently named, the bereavement trigger surfaced, and a shift toward treating the health anxiety/GAD (CBT, etc.) — with appropriate (not endless) safety-netting.

ice.ideas: Her symptoms mean a serious undiagnosed disease (brain tumour/MS); more scans/specialists will finally make her sure.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — a close friend died suddenly last year ("young and healthy"); she’s terrified the same will happen and leave her children motherless, and the checking/scan-seeking are attempts to control that terror.
ice.expectations: Another scan or a neurologist for certainty. What she actually needs: a validating explanation linking real symptoms to anxiety, the reassurance cycle named, the bereavement surfaced, and treatment of the health anxiety/GAD.

cues: Repeated normal tests + reassurance that never lasts + "things change, I need another scan" — the health-anxiety reassurance cycle.
Real somatic symptoms (palpitations, tingling, tension headache) + months of generalised worry — anxiety, not a tumour.
A friend who died suddenly last year — the bereavement trigger she hasn’t connected to her fear.

checkpoints.text: Recognises HEALTH ANXIETY (often with generalised anxiety disorder) from the pattern — repeated normal investigations, fleeting reassurance, bodily checking, catastrophic interpretation of benign somatic symptoms — rather than ordering another scan or onward referral for certainty

VALIDATES that the symptoms are REAL and explains the mechanism: anxiety genuinely causes palpitations, paraesthesia (hyperventilation), tension headaches and fatigue — so she is not "imagining it" or "wasting time", but the cause is anxiety, not a tumour/MS

Gently NAMES the reassurance/testing cycle: repeated tests and reassurance give brief relief but maintain the anxiety long-term, and another scan is unlikely to give lasting certainty — doing so without dismissing her or refusing all assessment of genuinely new symptoms

Surfaces and addresses the HIDDEN TRIGGER (the friend’s sudden death) and screens mood/risk (NICE CG123, 2011, withdrawn 2024: ask about anxiety directly — GAD-2 then GAD-7 — and look for depression, panic and risk to self); connects the bereavement and unprocessed grief/guilt to the onset of the health anxiety

Redirects to treatment of the anxiety in line with the NICE CG113 stepped-care model (psychoeducation and active monitoring; low-intensity help such as guided self-help; then CBT or applied relaxation, or an SSRI — sertraline first — if she chooses medication): psychological therapy (CBT adapted for health anxiety through NHS Talking Therapies), psychoeducation on the checking/Googling/reassurance-seeking maintaining factors, sleep; with sensible, bounded safety-netting (clear which genuinely new red-flag symptoms would warrant review)
Avoids both dismissiveness ("there’s nothing wrong, stop worrying") and collusion (endless scans); holds a warm, validating, confident stance that keeps her engaged and trusting
Explores the impact (exhaustion, marriage strain, shame) and the bereavement with compassion, framing treatment as getting her life back from the worry

Safety-nets proportionately and follows up: which specific NEW red-flag symptoms would warrant assessment (so she’s not abandoned), a referral for psychological therapy, an agreed plan to reduce checking/reassurance-seeking, and a follow-up that treats the anxiety as the diagnosis

worked.txt: "First, I want to be clear about something important: your symptoms are REAL. The racing heart, the tingling, the headaches, the exhaustion — you’re genuinely feeling all of those, you’re not imagining it and you’re not wasting my time. So let’s take them seriously and work out what’s actually causing them."

"Here’s the thing the scans have been telling us: your brain and body are fine on every test. What DOES cause exactly this combination — the palpitations, the tingling in your hands and face, the tension headaches, the tiredness — is anxiety. When we’re in a constant state of worry, the body pumps out adrenaline and we over-breathe, and that produces every single one of those symptoms. It’s not a tumour or MS; it’s anxiety, and that is genuinely good news because it’s very treatable."

"Can I gently point something out? Each scan calms you for a little while, then the worry comes back and latches onto the next symptom. That’s not a failing — it’s exactly how health anxiety works: reassurance feels great for a day, then fades, so we seek more. Another scan would do the same. The way out isn’t more tests; it’s treating the anxiety itself."

"Can I ask — when did all this really ramp up? … Your friend, who died suddenly last year. I’m so sorry. That makes complete sense of everything. When someone young and healthy dies out of the blue, it shatters the feeling that our bodies are safe, and the mind tries to regain control by checking and scanning for danger. Your fear isn’t random — it has a cause, and that’s something we can work with."

"So instead of another scan, what genuinely helps is a type of talking therapy designed for exactly this — it helps your mind stop sounding the alarm over normal body sensations, and gently reduces the checking and Googling that feed it. I can refer you. We can also talk about a medication that helps with anxiety if you’d like. This is the path that actually gives you lasting peace, not the next scan."

"And I’m not abandoning you or saying ‘never come back’. If you get genuinely NEW things — like weakness down one side, loss of vision, a sudden ‘worst-ever’ headache — those I’d want to see. But the day-to-day symptoms we now understand, and chasing them with scans keeps you trapped. Let’s treat the worry, get you sleeping, take the strain off you and your husband, and I’ll see you to follow this through. You deserve to feel safe in your own body again."

f.learning: Health anxiety (often with generalised anxiety disorder) presents as repeated normal investigations, fleetingly-effective reassurance, bodily checking and catastrophic interpretation of benign somatic symptoms — and the trap is to order another scan or refer for "certainty", which reinforces the cycle. The skill set: VALIDATE that the symptoms are real (anxiety genuinely causes palpitations, paraesthesia from hyperventilation, tension headaches and fatigue — she is not imagining it), explain the mechanism confidently, and gently NAME the reassurance/testing cycle (brief relief, long-term maintenance) without dismissing her or refusing to assess genuinely new red-flags. The examinable hidden agenda is the trigger — a close friend’s sudden death — which shattered her sense of bodily safety; surface it, connect it, screen mood/grief, and redirect to treatment in line with NICE CG113 stepped care (CBT adapted for health anxiety through NHS Talking Therapies, psychoeducation on checking/Googling/reassurance-seeking, sleep, consider an SSRI — sertraline first — if she chooses medication). Avoid both poles — dismissiveness ("nothing wrong, stop worrying") and collusion (endless scans) — and safety-net proportionately with specific new red-flag symptoms so she is treated, not abandoned.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG113 (2011) · NICE CG123 (2011; withdrawn May 2024) · NHS Talking Therapies · GMC Decision making and consent (2020)
knowledge.summary: Recurrent bodily symptoms, repeated normal tests and reassurance that never lasts point to health anxiety, often alongside generalised anxiety disorder. Treat the anxiety; do not order a test only to buy certainty.

points.t: Health anxiety: persistent fear of a serious illness, benign sensations read as danger, body checking, internet searching and reassurance-seeking that relieves the fear only briefly. Months of free-floating worry with restlessness, muscle tension, poor sleep, irritability and tiredness fit generalised anxiety disorder (NICE CG113).

Autonomic arousal and over-breathing cause palpitations, tingling in the hands and face, tension headache, dizziness and exhaustion. Say so clearly. Dismissing the symptoms breaks trust and drives more attendance.

points.h: Why more tests do not help
points.t: Each normal result calms the fear for a short time, then doubt returns and attaches to a new symptom. Testing for reassurance keeps the cycle going and adds the risk of incidental findings. Still examine and assess any genuinely new or red-flag feature on its own merits.

NICE CG123 (2011, withdrawn 2024): ask about anxiety directly (the GAD-2 questions are a quick start, then GAD-7) and look for depression, panic attacks and risk to self. Ask what started it: a bereavement or a health scare often precedes health anxiety, and the grief may need attention in its own right.

NICE CG113: psychoeducation and active monitoring first; then low-intensity help (guided self-help, psychoeducational groups); then CBT or applied relaxation, or an SSRI if she chooses medication. NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral and offers CBT adapted for health anxiety. Consider sertraline first if a drug is chosen (dose per BNF); explain early side effects and review soon after starting.

One named clinician, planned reviews rather than symptom-led visits, and an agreed short list of new symptoms that would need assessment. A request for a test the clinician judges not clinically indicated need not be granted, but explain why and offer a second opinion if she wants one (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

dg.d: Open question first; let her list her symptoms and her request for a scan without interrupting or arguing.
Generalised worry, sleep, irritability, the strain on her marriage, her children, and the shame of attending so often.
Reviewed the normal bloods, ECG and CT; GAD-7 and a mood screen; no further scan, with the reason explained.
Health anxiety with generalised anxiety disorder; tension-type headache; over-breathing as the cause of tingling; screened for depression and panic.
Asked about focal neurology, sudden severe headache, vomiting and visual loss; risk to self asked directly.
Named health anxiety and generalised anxiety clearly, linked to the bereavement, and explained how the symptoms are produced.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: CBT via NHS Talking Therapies, SSRI offered as an option (sertraline first per NICE CG113), bereavement support, and a practical step to cut checking.
Addressed sleep, the grief, the reassurance-seeking and the internet searching that keep the anxiety going.
Named clinician, planned review in weeks, specific new red-flag symptoms (999), and same-day contact if mood worsens.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “things change, don’t they?” and the months of worry; asked when it started and found the friend’s sudden death.
Idea (tumour or MS); concern (dying suddenly like her friend and leaving her children); expectation (another scan or a neurologist).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — a close friend died suddenly last year ("young and healthy"); she’s terrified the same will happen and leave her children motherless, and the checking/scan-seeking are attempts to control that terror — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mrs Karim, I’m Dr Lee. Thank you for joining. I can see you’re worried, so let’s start with you. Tell me what’s been happening and what’s on your mind today.
model.why: Open question and acknowledges her distress before any agenda

model.text: I know I’ve been in a lot. But this time I’m really worried — the headaches, my heart racing, the tingling, I’m exhausted. I’ve read it could be a brain tumour or MS. The scan was weeks ago, things change, don’t they? I need another scan, or a neurologist, just to be sure.

Thank you. I want to take every one of those symptoms seriously. Can I spend a few minutes understanding them properly, then we’ll talk about what’s causing them and what would genuinely help, including your question about a scan? Is that alright?
model.why: Sets an agenda that includes her request without promising it

model.text: Yes. Okay.
Tell me about the headaches. What are they like, and has anything about them changed recently?
model.why: Characterises the headache and screens for a genuine change

model.text: Like a tight band round my head. Most days. Worse when I’m stressed. Nothing sudden, it just builds.
Any weakness down one side, loss of vision, trouble speaking, a sudden severe headache, or being sick with them?
model.why: Rules out neurological red flags before reframing

model.text: No. None of that.
And the racing heart and the tingling — when do they come on?
model.why: Links the somatic symptoms to their trigger

model.text: When I’m lying there worrying, or after I’ve been reading about symptoms. My hands and round my mouth go pins and needles, and I feel like I can’t get a proper breath.
That’s very helpful. Can I ask about the rest of life? Beyond your health, do you find yourself worrying about lots of things, and how are sleep and your mood?
model.why: Screens for generalised anxiety, sleep and mood

model.text: Everything, really. I can’t switch off. I sleep badly, my shoulders are like concrete, I snap at everyone. It’s been months.
When things feel this heavy, some people feel low or hopeless, or even have thoughts of harming themselves. Has anything like that been happening for you?
model.why: Direct, normalised risk and depression screen

model.text: No, nothing like that. I’m just frightened all the time.
Can I ask when this really started to ramp up? Was there anything around that time?
model.why: Opens the door to the trigger without leading

model.text: (Pause.) My friend died last year. Out of nowhere. A bleed in her brain. She was young, she was healthy. One day she was fine.
I’m so sorry. That must have been a terrible shock. When you feel a headache or your heart racing now, what goes through your mind?
model.why: Responds to the loss, then links it to her fear

model.text: That it’s happening to me. That I’ll just go, like she did, and my children won’t have a mum. So I check. I Google. I come here. And my husband says I’m obsessed.

That makes complete sense of everything you’ve told me. You’re not being silly. Losing her took away your sense that your body is safe, and all the checking is your mind trying to get it back. It sounds exhausting, for you and at home.
model.why: Validates, names the impact and the meaning without judgement

model.text: (Tearful.) It is. I feel ashamed. I just want to feel normal.

Let me explain what I think is going on. Your symptoms are real. When the mind is on constant alert, the body releases adrenaline and we breathe faster without noticing. That causes a racing heart, tingling in the hands and round the mouth, tight-band headaches and tiredness. Your tests show your brain and heart are healthy. What’s causing this is anxiety, and anxiety is very treatable.
model.why: Validates the symptoms and explains the mechanism with confidence

model.text: But how can you be sure it isn’t something the scan missed?

That’s a fair question. Can I point something out, gently? After each test you felt better for a little while, then the doubt came back and fixed on something new. That’s how health anxiety works. Another scan would most likely do the same — a few days of relief, then more worry. So I don’t think another scan is the right thing for you, and I’d rather offer something that actually lasts.
model.why: Names the reassurance cycle and declines the scan with reasons

model.text: (Quietly.) That is what happens. Every time.

What helps most is a talking therapy called CBT, designed for exactly this. It helps your mind stop sounding the alarm over normal body sensations and cuts down the checking and Googling that feed it. You can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies, or I can give you the details today. Some people also find a medicine for anxiety helpful. Would you like to hear about that too?
model.why: Offers evidence-based treatment and a choice

model.text: I’d like to try the therapy first. I’m not sure about tablets.

That’s a very reasonable choice. We can talk about a tablet at the review if you want to. And the grief for your friend matters too — would you be open to talking about her with the therapist, or with bereavement support?
model.why: Respects her choice and addresses the bereavement in the plan

model.text: I’ve never really talked about her. Maybe I should.

One experiment for the next two weeks: when the urge to check or Google comes, write the worry down and wait before acting on it. And I’d like you to see me, the same doctor, at planned reviews rather than whenever a symptom scares you. Would that work?
model.why: One concrete, owned step and consistent follow-up

model.text: I can try. Seeing you each time would help.

I’m not saying never come back. If you had something genuinely new — weakness down one side, loss of vision, trouble speaking, or a sudden, severe ‘worst ever’ headache — that’s 999. Those are different from what you have now. And if your mood dipped or you felt unsafe, contact us the same day.
model.why: Bounded, specific safety-net so she is not abandoned

model.text: Okay. That’s clearer than I expected.
So when your husband asks tonight what the doctor said, what will you tell him?
model.why: Teach-back checks the new explanation has landed

model.text: That it’s real, but it’s anxiety, not a tumour. That I’m doing the therapy, trying not to Google, and seeing you in three weeks.
That’s exactly it. I’ll book you in with me in three weeks. You’ve been carrying a lot since your friend died, and you deserve to feel safe in your own body again.
model.why: Closes warmly with a booked, named follow-up

social.t: Months of worry and checking are straining her marriage, and the fear centres on her children. Treatment framed as getting her family life back tends to engage better than a diagnosis alone.
A friend’s sudden death shattered her sense of safety. Unprocessed grief can drive health anxiety; offer bereavement support alongside CBT.

legal.t: A patient cannot insist on an investigation the doctor judges not clinically indicated. Explain the reasons, record the discussion and offer a second opinion if she asks (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Fragmented care across many clinicians and private providers leads to repeated tests. A named clinician with planned reviews protects her from harm and supports good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Avoid “nothing wrong” and “in your head”. Coding health anxiety or generalised anxiety accurately helps the next clinician avoid repeating the cycle; explain to her what is recorded.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), Anxiety UK and Mind for self-help resources, and Cruse Bereavement Support for grief.

redFlags: Focal neurology, visual loss, speech disturbance or a sudden severe headache — genuinely new features that need assessment
Headache with vomiting or a change in character (worse lying flat, waking her) — assess on its own merits
Low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm — ask directly
psychosocial: Months of generalised worry, poor sleep, muscle tension and irritability
Impact on her marriage, her children and her sense of control; shame about attending
Checking, internet searching and reassurance-seeking as the behaviours that maintain the fear
ice: Idea: a brain tumour or MS that the last scan might have missed
Concern: dying suddenly like her friend and leaving her children without a mother
Expectation: another scan or a neurologist to be completely sure

playbook.diagnosis: Give a positive diagnosis rather than a list of negatives: “Your symptoms are real, and they fit anxiety — health anxiety alongside a more general anxiety that’s been building for months. The tests tell us your brain and heart are healthy.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of a smoke alarm that’s become too sensitive — it goes off for burnt toast as loudly as for a fire. Your body’s alarm has been turned up since your friend died. The alarm is real and noisy, but there’s no fire. Treatment turns the sensitivity back down.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been frightened that what happened to your friend will happen to you and your children will be left without you. That fear makes complete sense, and it’s exactly what we’re going to treat.”
management.psychosocial: Build the grief and the strain at home into the plan: bereavement support, CBT that targets checking and reassurance-seeking, and one practical step she chooses (delay before checking or searching).
sharedPlan: No further scan or referral for reassurance; reasons explained and documented
CBT for health anxiety via NHS Talking Therapies; SSRI offered as an option (NICE CG113)
Bereavement support; named clinician with planned reviews
safetyNet: 999 for new focal weakness, visual loss, speech disturbance or a sudden severe headache
Same-day contact if mood falls or she feels unsafe; review with the same GP in three weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed at either extreme: ordering the scan to end the conversation, or dismissing a frightened woman with “your tests are normal”. The marks sit in the middle — a confident diagnosis, the trigger found, and a real treatment offered.

items.fail: Agreeing to another scan or a neurology referral “just to be sure”.
items.why: Testing for reassurance maintains health anxiety and adds harm from incidental findings. Examiners read it as avoiding the real problem: “management plan not appropriate for the working diagnosis”.
items.fix: Decline with reasons and offer something better: “Each test has helped for a few days. I’d rather give you something that lasts.”

items.fail: “Your tests are all normal, so there’s nothing to worry about.”
items.why: Denying real symptoms ruptures trust — “does not show understanding of the patient’s perspective”. She will simply book again.
items.fix: Validate first, then explain the mechanism: adrenaline, over-breathing, muscle tension. A real cause for real symptoms.

items.fail: Never asking when it started, so the friend’s death stays hidden.
items.why: The trigger is the key to the diagnosis and to engagement. Missing it is “does not identify the patient’s underlying agenda”.
items.fix: “When did this really ramp up — was anything happening in your life then?” Then link the loss to the fear.

items.fail: Labelling it anxiety without a mood or risk screen.
items.why: Depression and risk commonly coexist with months of anxiety. Omitting them is a safety gap.
items.fix: One normalised, direct question about low mood and thoughts of self-harm, and a GAD-7 to measure progress.

items.fail: Closing with “come back if you’re worried” — or its opposite, “you don’t need to keep coming in”.
items.why: Open-ended reassurance feeds symptom-led visits; a blanket brush-off abandons her. Both are unsafe safety-netting.
items.fix: Name the few new symptoms that need assessment, then book planned reviews with the same clinician.

items.fail: A lecture on CBT, SSRIs and sleep hygiene in the final minute, with no choice offered.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient in the management plan.” A list without choice rarely leads to action.
items.fix: Offer the options, let her choose, and agree one small step she owns — delay before checking or searching.

timeMap.d: She arrives with a list and a request. Let her finish. Promise to take the symptoms seriously and to discuss the scan, without agreeing to it.
Headache character and neurological red flags; when the palpitations and tingling happen; generalised worry, sleep, tension, mood and risk.
“When did this really ramp up?” The friend’s sudden death and the fear for her children surface here. Validate before explaining.
Real symptoms, anxiety as the cause, the reassurance cycle named kindly. No scan, with reasons. CBT, optional SSRI, bereavement support, one step to reduce checking.
Bounded red flags (999), same-day contact if mood drops, named follow-up in three weeks. Teach-back: “What will you tell your husband?”

wordPics.fail: Orders another scan or refers to neurology for reassurance; or says “there’s nothing wrong with you” and ends the call; never asks when it started, so misses the friend’s death; no mood or risk screen; no treatment offered for the anxiety.
wordPics.pass: Screens for neurological red flags; recognises health anxiety and generalised anxiety; explains that the symptoms are real and caused by anxiety; declines further tests with reasons; offers CBT and a follow-up with a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds the bereavement and links it to her fear of leaving her children; names the reassurance cycle in her own words; offers stepped treatment with genuine choice; agrees one owned step to reduce checking; sets a named clinician and planned reviews; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “All your tests are normal, so there’s nothing wrong with you.”
avoid.instead: “Your symptoms are real. The tests show your brain and heart are healthy — what’s causing this is anxiety, and that’s treatable.”
avoid.why: Dismissing the symptoms loses her trust and sends her to the next appointment.

avoid.dont: “Fine, I’ll refer you to neurology just to put your mind at rest.”
avoid.instead: “Each test has helped for a few days, then the worry came back. I’d rather offer something that lasts.”
avoid.why: Testing for reassurance feeds the cycle; examiners mark it as collusion, not kindness.

avoid.dont: “You just need to stop Googling and try to relax.”
avoid.instead: “Checking and searching keep the alarm going. CBT helps you step out of that, and I can help you get it.”
avoid.why: An instruction without a mechanism or a treatment offer earns no Tasks marks.

Tell me about the headaches. What are they like, and has anything about them changed recently?
SCA_MODELS.why: Characterises the headache and screens for a genuine change

SCA_MODELS.text: Like a tight band round my head. Most days. Worse when I’m stressed. Nothing sudden, it just builds.
Any weakness down one side, loss of vision, trouble speaking, a sudden severe headache, or being sick with them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Rules out neurological red flags before reframing

SCA_MODELS.text: No. None of that.
And the racing heart and the tingling — when do they come on?
SCA_MODELS.why: Links the somatic symptoms to their trigger

SCA_MODELS.text: When I’m lying there worrying, or after I’ve been reading about symptoms. My hands and round my mouth go pins and needles, and I feel like I can’t get a proper breath.
That’s very helpful. Can I ask about the rest of life? Beyond your health, do you find yourself worrying about lots of things, and how are sleep and your mood?
SCA_MODELS.why: Screens for generalised anxiety, sleep and mood

SCA_MODELS.text: Everything, really. I can’t switch off. I sleep badly, my shoulders are like concrete, I snap at everyone. It’s been months.
When things feel this heavy, some people feel low or hopeless, or even have thoughts of harming themselves. Has anything like that been happening for you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Direct, normalised risk and depression screen

SCA_MODELS.text: No, nothing like that. I’m just frightened all the time.
Can I ask when this really started to ramp up? Was there anything around that time?
SCA_MODELS.why: Opens the door to the trigger without leading

SCA_MODELS.text: (Pause.) My friend died last year. Out of nowhere. A bleed in her brain. She was young, she was healthy. One day she was fine.
I’m so sorry. That must have been a terrible shock. When you feel a headache or your heart racing now, what goes through your mind?
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to the loss, then links it to her fear

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s happening to me. That I’ll just go, like she did, and my children won’t have a mum. So I check. I Google. I come here. And my husband says I’m obsessed.

That makes complete sense of everything you’ve told me. You’re not being silly. Losing her took away your sense that your body is safe, and all the checking is your mind trying to get it back. It sounds exhausting, for you and at home.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates, names the impact and the meaning without judgement

SCA_MODELS.text: (Tearful.) It is. I feel ashamed. I just want to feel normal.

Let me explain what I think is going on. Your symptoms are real. When the mind is on constant alert, the body releases adrenaline and we breathe faster without noticing. That causes a racing heart, tingling in the hands and round the mouth, tight-band headaches and tiredness. Your tests show your brain and heart are healthy. What’s causing this is anxiety, and anxiety is very treatable.
SCA_MODELS.why: Validates the symptoms and explains the mechanism with confidence

SCA_MODELS.text: But how can you be sure it isn’t something the scan missed?

That’s a fair question. Can I point something out, gently? After each test you felt better for a little while, then the doubt came back and fixed on something new. That’s how health anxiety works. Another scan would most likely do the same — a few days of relief, then more worry. So I don’t think another scan is the right thing for you, and I’d rather offer something that actually lasts.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the reassurance cycle and declines the scan with reasons

SCA_MODELS.text: (Quietly.) That is what happens. Every time.

What helps most is a talking therapy called CBT, designed for exactly this. It helps your mind stop sounding the alarm over normal body sensations and cuts down the checking and Googling that feed it. You can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies, or I can give you the details today. Some people also find a medicine for anxiety helpful. Would you like to hear about that too?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers evidence-based treatment and a choice

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d like to try the therapy first. I’m not sure about tablets.

That’s a very reasonable choice. We can talk about a tablet at the review if you want to. And the grief for your friend matters too — would you be open to talking about her with the therapist, or with bereavement support?
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects her choice and addresses the bereavement in the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ve never really talked about her. Maybe I should.

One experiment for the next two weeks: when the urge to check or Google comes, write the worry down and wait before acting on it. And I’d like you to see me, the same doctor, at planned reviews rather than whenever a symptom scares you. Would that work?
SCA_MODELS.why: One concrete, owned step and consistent follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: I can try. Seeing you each time would help.

I’m not saying never come back. If you had something genuinely new — weakness down one side, loss of vision, trouble speaking, or a sudden, severe ‘worst ever’ headache — that’s 999. Those are different from what you have now. And if your mood dipped or you felt unsafe, contact us the same day.
SCA_MODELS.why: Bounded, specific safety-net so she is not abandoned

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s clearer than I expected.
So when your husband asks tonight what the doctor said, what will you tell him?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back checks the new explanation has landed

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s real, but it’s anxiety, not a tumour. That I’m doing the therapy, trying not to Google, and seeing you in three weeks.
That’s exactly it. I’ll book you in with me in three weeks. You’ve been carrying a lot since your friend died, and you deserve to feel safe in your own body again.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes warmly with a booked, named follow-up

SCA_STEM.name: Nadia Karim
pmh: Frequent attender: several recent appointments with headaches, palpitations, tingling and fatigue
SCA_STEM.recent: Recent investigations all normal: blood tests and ECG in the practice; a CT head arranged privately, reported as normal. No mental health diagnosis coded.
SCA_STEM.reason: Booked a video appointment about headaches, palpitations, tingling and tiredness. Asking for another scan or a neurology referral.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE CG113 (2011) · NICE CG123 (2011; withdrawn May 2024) · NHS Talking Therapies · GMC Decision making and consent (2020)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Recurrent bodily symptoms, repeated normal tests and reassurance that never lasts point to health anxiety, often alongside generalised anxiety disorder. Treat the anxiety; do not order a test only to buy certainty.

points.t: Health anxiety: persistent fear of a serious illness, benign sensations read as danger, body checking, internet searching and reassurance-seeking that relieves the fear only briefly. Months of free-floating worry with restlessness, muscle tension, poor sleep, irritability and tiredness fit generalised anxiety disorder (NICE CG113).

Autonomic arousal and over-breathing cause palpitations, tingling in the hands and face, tension headache, dizziness and exhaustion. Say so clearly. Dismissing the symptoms breaks trust and drives more attendance.

points.h: Why more tests do not help
points.t: Each normal result calms the fear for a short time, then doubt returns and attaches to a new symptom. Testing for reassurance keeps the cycle going and adds the risk of incidental findings. Still examine and assess any genuinely new or red-flag feature on its own merits.

NICE CG123 (2011, withdrawn 2024): ask about anxiety directly (the GAD-2 questions are a quick start, then GAD-7) and look for depression, panic attacks and risk to self. Ask what started it: a bereavement or a health scare often precedes health anxiety, and the grief may need attention in its own right.

NICE CG113: psychoeducation and active monitoring first; then low-intensity help (guided self-help, psychoeducational groups); then CBT or applied relaxation, or an SSRI if she chooses medication. NHS Talking Therapies accepts self-referral and offers CBT adapted for health anxiety. Consider sertraline first if a drug is chosen (dose per BNF); explain early side effects and review soon after starting.

One named clinician, planned reviews rather than symptom-led visits, and an agreed short list of new symptoms that would need assessment. A request for a test the clinician judges not clinically indicated need not be granted, but explain why and offer a second opinion if she wants one (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let her list her symptoms and her request for a scan without interrupting or arguing.
Generalised worry, sleep, irritability, the strain on her marriage, her children, and the shame of attending so often.
Picked up “things change, don’t they?” and the months of worry; asked when it started and found the friend’s sudden death.
Idea (tumour or MS); concern (dying suddenly like her friend and leaving her children); expectation (another scan or a neurologist).
Reviewed the normal bloods, ECG and CT; GAD-7 and a mood screen; no further scan, with the reason explained.
Health anxiety with generalised anxiety disorder; tension-type headache; over-breathing as the cause of tingling; screened for depression and panic.
Asked about focal neurology, sudden severe headache, vomiting and visual loss; risk to self asked directly.
Named health anxiety and generalised anxiety clearly, linked to the bereavement, and explained how the symptoms are produced.
CBT via NHS Talking Therapies, SSRI offered as an option (sertraline first per NICE CG113), bereavement support, and a practical step to cut checking.
Addressed sleep, the grief, the reassurance-seeking and the internet searching that keep the anxiety going.
Named clinician, planned review in weeks, specific new red-flag symptoms (999), and same-day contact if mood worsens.

social.t: Months of worry and checking are straining her marriage, and the fear centres on her children. Treatment framed as getting her family life back tends to engage better than a diagnosis alone.
A friend’s sudden death shattered her sense of safety. Unprocessed grief can drive health anxiety; offer bereavement support alongside CBT.

legal.t: A patient cannot insist on an investigation the doctor judges not clinically indicated. Explain the reasons, record the discussion and offer a second opinion if she asks (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: Fragmented care across many clinicians and private providers leads to repeated tests. A named clinician with planned reviews protects her from harm and supports good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Avoid “nothing wrong” and “in your head”. Coding health anxiety or generalised anxiety accurately helps the next clinician avoid repeating the cycle; explain to her what is recorded.

community.t: NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral), Anxiety UK and Mind for self-help resources, and Cruse Bereavement Support for grief.

redFlags: Focal neurology, visual loss, speech disturbance or a sudden severe headache — genuinely new features that need assessment
Headache with vomiting or a change in character (worse lying flat, waking her) — assess on its own merits
Low mood, hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm — ask directly
psychosocial: Months of generalised worry, poor sleep, muscle tension and irritability
Impact on her marriage, her children and her sense of control; shame about attending
Checking, internet searching and reassurance-seeking as the behaviours that maintain the fear
ice: Idea: a brain tumour or MS that the last scan might have missed
Concern: dying suddenly like her friend and leaving her children without a mother
Expectation: another scan or a neurologist to be completely sure

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Give a positive diagnosis rather than a list of negatives: “Your symptoms are real, and they fit anxiety — health anxiety alongside a more general anxiety that’s been building for months. The tests tell us your brain and heart are healthy.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of a smoke alarm that’s become too sensitive — it goes off for burnt toast as loudly as for a fire. Your body’s alarm has been turned up since your friend died. The alarm is real and noisy, but there’s no fire. Treatment turns the sensitivity back down.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been frightened that what happened to your friend will happen to you and your children will be left without you. That fear makes complete sense, and it’s exactly what we’re going to treat.”
management.psychosocial: Build the grief and the strain at home into the plan: bereavement support, CBT that targets checking and reassurance-seeking, and one practical step she chooses (delay before checking or searching).
sharedPlan: No further scan or referral for reassurance; reasons explained and documented
CBT for health anxiety via NHS Talking Therapies; SSRI offered as an option (NICE CG113)
Bereavement support; named clinician with planned reviews
safetyNet: 999 for new focal weakness, visual loss, speech disturbance or a sudden severe headache
Same-day contact if mood falls or she feels unsafe; review with the same GP in three weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed at either extreme: ordering the scan to end the conversation, or dismissing a frightened woman with “your tests are normal”. The marks sit in the middle — a confident diagnosis, the trigger found, and a real treatment offered.

items.fail: Agreeing to another scan or a neurology referral “just to be sure”.
items.why: Testing for reassurance maintains health anxiety and adds harm from incidental findings. Examiners read it as avoiding the real problem: “management plan not appropriate for the working diagnosis”.
items.fix: Decline with reasons and offer something better: “Each test has helped for a few days. I’d rather give you something that lasts.”

items.fail: “Your tests are all normal, so there’s nothing to worry about.”
items.why: Denying real symptoms ruptures trust — “does not show understanding of the patient’s perspective”. She will simply book again.
items.fix: Validate first, then explain the mechanism: adrenaline, over-breathing, muscle tension. A real cause for real symptoms.

items.fail: Never asking when it started, so the friend’s death stays hidden.
items.why: The trigger is the key to the diagnosis and to engagement. Missing it is “does not identify the patient’s underlying agenda”.
items.fix: “When did this really ramp up — was anything happening in your life then?” Then link the loss to the fear.

items.fail: Labelling it anxiety without a mood or risk screen.
items.why: Depression and risk commonly coexist with months of anxiety. Omitting them is a safety gap.
items.fix: One normalised, direct question about low mood and thoughts of self-harm, and a GAD-7 to measure progress.

items.fail: Closing with “come back if you’re worried” — or its opposite, “you don’t need to keep coming in”.
items.why: Open-ended reassurance feeds symptom-led visits; a blanket brush-off abandons her. Both are unsafe safety-netting.
items.fix: Name the few new symptoms that need assessment, then book planned reviews with the same clinician.

items.fail: A lecture on CBT, SSRIs and sleep hygiene in the final minute, with no choice offered.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient in the management plan.” A list without choice rarely leads to action.
items.fix: Offer the options, let her choose, and agree one small step she owns — delay before checking or searching.
